opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think this is one of the more underappreciated framing choices in how people do RL on language models right now. In classical RL, you think of every token as an action, so a completion is a long trajectory of many little decisions. But in practice, with something like GRPO or the outcome-based reward setups people use for reasoning models, you sample a whole completion, score it at the end, right or wrong, and push up or down the log-probability of the entire sequence. Functionally, you're treating the whole completion as one big action in what's basically a contextual bandit.

Why does that matter for credit assignment? Because you're giving up any attempt to say which part of the reasoning was good. Say the model writes two thousand tokens of chain of thought, makes a brilliant move on line three, a dumb arithmetic slip on line forty, and somehow still lands on the right answer. Every one of those tokens gets reinforced the same amount. The signal is extremely coarse. One scalar is spread across thousands of decisions.

The surprising thing is that it works anyway, and I think that tells us something. It works because the pretrained model is already a very strong prior. You're not searching from scratch; you're reweighting a distribution that already puts real probability on good reasoning. Across many samples, the noise from crediting irrelevant or bad tokens averages out, and what's consistently correlated with success, like checking your work or backtracking when something looks off, gets amplified. So the bandit framing is crude, but the prior makes it sample-efficient enough.

The flip side is that it's probably why these methods are so data- and compute-hungry, and why they struggle as horizons get longer. If you go from a two-thousand-token math problem to an agent doing hours of work with tool calls, one scalar at the end becomes a really weak signal for which of thousands of steps mattered. Eventually you need something better: value functions that work at the token or step level, process rewards, or the model learning to critique its own intermediate steps. Classical RL gave us a lot of tools for temporal credit assignment, and the current recipe mostly ignores them.

So I see it as a pragmatic simplification that pays off in the regime we're in now, but it's also a pretty clear sign of where the next bottleneck is. Whoever cracks fine-grained credit assignment for long-horizon LLM behavior without the instability that comes with learned critics will unlock a lot.

r001.rationale: The response explains that one episode-level score is spread across all tokens, making credit coarse, but it does not identify interactions among token-level terms as a source of the attribution difficulty.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the thing people miss is that when you do RLHF on a language model, the "action" in the RL sense isn't a token. It's the whole completion. The model emits a few hundred or a few thousand tokens, and then at the very end a reward model or a verifier says "good" or "bad," and that single scalar gets smeared back over everything that was generated.

That's a really strange regime if you come from classical RL. In Atari or in robotics, you take an action, you get a reward, you take another action, you get another reward. The horizon is long and the feedback is dense enough that the temporal credit assignment problem is about figuring out which of your many small decisions mattered. In the LLM setup, you've effectively collapsed the horizon to one. You took one giant action, you got one number. So in a sense credit assignment across time just disappears. There's no "which step was it" question, because there's only one step.

But that doesn't mean the problem went away. It got pushed down into the network. Now the hard part is figuring out which of the thousands of tokens inside that single action were actually responsible for the outcome, and the only machinery you have for that is backprop through the policy gradient. You're asking the gradient to do what the reward structure used to do for you. And a policy gradient with a terminal reward is a pretty blunt instrument. The variance is high, and every token in a successful trajectory gets reinforced about equally, including the ones that were irrelevant or even slightly wrong but happened to be followed by a correct answer.

So the consequence is twofold. On one hand, it's kind of liberating. You don't need per-step reward shaping, you don't need a value function over intermediate states that's any good, you can just score the outcome. That's a big reason outcome-based RL on math and code has worked as well as it has. On the other hand, it means the amount you can learn per episode is bounded by one bit-ish of information, and you're relying heavily on the pretrained prior to make the search tractable. The model already more or less knows how to write the proof. RL is just nudging the distribution toward the completions that happen to land.

The place this becomes really consequential is when you start caring about longer horizons that actually do span multiple actions. Agents that take an action, observe the world, take another action. Now you're back in the regime where you have to decide what the unit of credit is. Do you treat each tool call as an action? Each whole turn? The entire multi-hour task? Those choices change what the gradient is able to see. If you make the action too big, you're back to one scalar for an enormous amount of behavior and the signal gets diluted. If you make it too small, you need something like a value function to give you intermediate guidance, and we're honestly not that good at learning value functions in these open-ended settings.

So I think of "one completion is one action" as a design decision that got baked in early because it was convenient for chat, and we're now discovering that a lot of the hard problems in agentic RL are really just the credit assignment problem resurfacing once that convenient collapse stops being available.

r001.rationale: The response says a terminal reward makes it hard to identify which tokens caused the outcome, but it does not identify interactions among token-level terms as a source of that difficulty.

astra-6.text:
Because you’re choosing the granularity at which the learner gets told what worked. A completion might contain thousands of tokens, but if you treat it as one action, you get a reward for that whole sequence. That reward doesn’t tell you which intermediate decisions were responsible for the outcome.

Say the model has the right strategy, makes one arithmetic error, and gets the wrong answer. A low reward doesn’t distinguish that from a completely misguided strategy. Conversely, if it gets the answer right, that doesn’t mean every step it took was useful. You can still learn from an outcome reward, but you have to infer those distinctions across many samples.

And even if your implementation computes gradients for each token, that doesn’t automatically solve the problem. If every token gets the same sequence-level advantage, you’re still giving a very coarse credit signal. The consequential question is whether you can estimate how an intermediate decision changes the probability of eventual success. That’s what lets you reinforce the useful parts of a trajectory without having to reinforce the whole thing indiscriminately.

r001.rationale: The response says a sequence-level reward or shared advantage gives a coarse signal that does not identify useful intermediate decisions. It does not identify interactions among token-level terms as a source of the credit-assignment difficulty.

sol-6.1.text:
Because an action is usually something you get to assign credit to individually. If you treat an entire completion as one action, you might generate thousands of tokens, get a single reward at the end, and then have to figure out which parts of that sequence were responsible for the outcome.

Suppose the model has the right approach but makes one arithmetic mistake halfway through. A negative reward doesn’t tell you whether the approach was bad, the arithmetic was bad, or the final answer was formatted incorrectly. You can still learn from that signal, but it’s a much harder credit-assignment problem.

And the distinction is partly hidden by how we describe the system. At the API level, a completion looks like one action. Internally, it’s a long sequence of decisions. Calling it one action doesn’t eliminate the temporal structure; it just pushes the credit-assignment problem inside that action.

r001.rationale: The response explains that a single end-of-completion reward makes it hard to identify which parts of the sequence caused the outcome, but it does not identify interactions among token-level terms as a source of that difficulty.
